clinicalPearls: Typically a unilateral, broad-based or pedunculated lesion at the mid-membranous vocal fold, arising from phonotrauma or acute vocal overuse
Presents with persistent hoarseness, breathiness, vocal fatigue, and sometimes a sensation of a lump or the need to clear the throat
May be haemorrhagic (following an episode of forceful voicing) or translucent and gelatinous in appearance
Distinguished from vocal nodules, which are usually bilateral and symmetrical and respond better to voice therapy alone
Videostroboscopy shows disruption of the mucosal wave over the lesion and incomplete glottic closure
Smoking and laryngopharyngeal reflux act as aggravating cofactors and should be addressed
Established polyps commonly require microlaryngeal surgical excision with preservation of the vocal ligament, followed by voice rest and therapy
reference.pathophysiology: A vocal fold polyp develops when repeated or violent phonotrauma injures the microvasculature of the superficial lamina propria (Reinke's space), producing localised submucosal oedema, fibrin exudation, and sometimes haemorrhage. Over time the exudate organises into a discrete, often pedunculated mass covered by epithelium. The lesion adds mass and stiffness to the vibrating edge, disturbing the mucosal wave and preventing complete glottic closure, which produces the characteristic breathy, rough voice. Smoking, vocal misuse, and reflux-related mucosal irritation promote and perpetuate the process.
additionalInvestigations: Flexible fibreoptic laryngoscopy to visualise the lesion and assess mobility
Videostroboscopy to characterise the mucosal wave and glottic closure
Perceptual and acoustic voice assessment by a speech and language therapist
Histological examination of any excised specimen to exclude dysplasia or malignancy
redFlags: A firm, irregular, or leukoplakic lesion in a smoker raising concern for malignancy
Impaired vocal fold mobility, which is not expected with a benign polyp
Progressive dysphonia unresponsive to conservative measures
Cervical lymphadenopathy accompanying a laryngeal lesion
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent; small early polyps may regress with voice therapy and control of aggravating factors, and surgically excised polyps rarely recur when phonotrauma, smoking, and reflux are addressed, with restoration of a near-normal voice in most patients.
pitfalls: Assuming any exophytic vocal fold lesion is benign without stroboscopy and, where excised, histology
Proceeding to surgery without correcting the underlying vocal behaviour, leading to recurrence
Overlooking coexisting reflux or smoking as perpetuating factors
Confusing a unilateral polyp with bilateral nodules and mismanaging with therapy alone
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
